title: What's the buzz around polyploids? Plant–pollinator interactions among sympatric cytotypes in an African grassland bulb
content:
Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.


Abstract

Polyploidisation is one of the primary ways by which instantaneous speciation may occur, since it has the potential to result in immediate reproductive isolation. Prezygotic reproductive isolation between diploids and polyploids can arise through differences in pollinator interactions among cytotypes, either as a direct consequence of polyploidisation-induced changes to pollinator signalling structures and traits, or due to post-polyploidisation selection. Here we assess whether reproductively isolated sympatric diploids and polyploids of the African grassland geophyte, Oxalis obliquifolia, have different pollinator assemblages, or in the case of shared pollinators, whether there are differences in pollinator visitation rates between cytotypes. A pollinator visitation experiment was conducted by placing diploid, tetraploid and hexaploid plants into a natural grassland habitat, using a randomised block design. Pollinator interactions were then monitored over the course of two consecutive flowering seasons, using 30-min observation sessions for each block. Each insect visitor was recorded and voucher specimens were collected for identification and inspected for the presence of O. obliquifolia pollen using light microscopy. Potential species-level specialisation among pollinators and cytotypes was determined using the standardised Kullback–Leibler distance and network specialisation using a standard two-dimensional Shannon entropy index. Differences in visitation rates were assessed using GLMMs. Pollinators may not distinguish between diploids and polyploids, with all cytotypes being visited by all pollinators at appreciable rates. The species-level and network specialisation indices support generalist interactions. The most common pollinator, Ceratina nyassensis, shows a significant, if slight, preference for larger polyploid flowers. Pollinators are shared among experimentally co-occurring cytotypes, and pollen is likely being vectored between ploidies in mixed ploidy populations if similar pollinator visitation occurs in naturally mixed-cytotype populations. Therefore, pollinator-mediated assortative mating may not be the most likely mechanism supporting cytotype reproductive isolation. Other prezygotic and postzygotic isolating mechanisms, such as pollen rejection by the stigma, problems with pollen tube formation and endosperm chromosome imbalances, are potentially more likely to play a role.
